newsitem.title: BOSNIA: IFOR security headaches won't end with elections.
newsitem.headline: IFOR security headaches won't end with elections.

text.p: For NATO forces in Moslem-controlled northwestern Bosnia, the security headaches won't end when the polling stations close on Saturday night after nationwide elections.
Local detachments of the Bosnian peace implementation force (IFOR) believe that their greatest test may not come on polling day but when winners and losers are declared up to two weeks later.
The Canadian-led multinational brigades responsible for the Moslem-controlled Bihac pocket and adjoining Serb-controlled territory plan a major security operation for Saturday.

Their prime aims are to ensure that arms of the warring factions remain under lock and key and to keep roads open so that voters can get to polling stations. But they are not planning to relax their vigilance when the stations close.

"Getting the results out is going to be another interesting time," said Captain Chris Lemay, spokesman for the multinational brigade which also includes troops from Britain and the Czech republic -- a would-be NATO member.
Bihac, which the Serbs besieged for more than three years, has a problem unique to Bosnia. Here Moslems are set against fellow Moslems and emotions are high.
Local Moslem businessmen turned warlord Fikret Abdic broke away from the Bosnian government in the northern part of the Bihac enclave and struck deals with both the Serbs and Croats.
The deals won Abdic's rebel area relative peace and reasonable food supplies, while fellow Moslems in Bihac town only 40 km (25 miles) to the south were near starvation.
But they also earned him the enduring hatred of the Moslem-led government, which has put him on trial as a war criminal while many local Moslems regard him as a traitor.
On Thursday local police blocked Abdic's only attempt to return from his home in exile in Croatia to stage an election rally in his former stronghold of Velika Kladusa.
"There is a certain uneasiness with Abdic's supporters in our region," said Lemay, who comes from Quebec town of Trois Rivieres. "They might use violence when the results come out."
Abdic, who was driven out of the country by government forces last year, is running for the three-man Bosnian presidency and his party is also contesting the polls.
Lemay, based in rudimentary quarters next to a muddy cement factory, may be understating things. That "uneasiness" has erupted into violence on a number of occasions in recent weeks.
In the worst incident, a grenade lobbed into the home of an Abdic supporter seriously injured a young girl. A man was arrested for the attack but later inexplicably released.
International officials, bound to impartiality, are reluctant to comment about the incidents of thuggery.
But one, who requested anonymity, said the ruling Democratic Action Party (SDA) of President Alija Izetbegovic seems unable to tolerate even the weak opposition it faces.
Local SDA officials at polling stations would know exactly who the opposition supporters were. Many people were frightened to turn up to vote for other parties for fear of retribution.
"If you don't support the SDA, it's best to stay away," said the official.
Other opposition parties, including one led by former prime minister Haris Silajdzic, have alleged a dirty tricks campaign to stop their rallies in the Velika Kladusa area.

On one occasion a cinema booked for a rally was mysteriously closed "for renovation". In another town, a mayor summoned local people to a hastily-called meeting just before the opposition was due to hold a rally in the same hall.
"No one turned up to the rally. Not even the local dog," said the official.
